summary:
Ağrı stands under the national legal framework of Türkiye; the source inventory records no province-specific statute, ordinance or incident series applying to the province. What a trans visitor encounters in Ağrı is Turkish national law and national police practice.

Human Rights Watch reported on 29 October 2025 that a leaked draft of Türkiye's omnibus 11th Judicial Package would open the way to criminal charges against LGBT people, described there as one of the most alarming rollbacks of rights in decades. Conduct deemed 'contrary to biological sex and general morality', including its so-called 'promotion', would carry up to three years in prison, and participation in same-sex engagement or marriage ceremonies up to four years. Same-sex marriage is not legal in Türkiye, so such ceremonies are symbolic by definition. The package contains no provision naming Ağrı.

The same draft would restrict gender-affirming care: the surgery age raised from 18 to 25, permanent infertility made mandatory, medical professionals fined or imprisoned for up to seven years, and transgender patients imprisoned for up to three years for care falling outside the new limits. Human Rights Watch warns this would push transition treatment into underground settings. A trans visitor seeking or already receiving hormone therapy should expect that any care sought in Türkiye now sits under these proposed constraints.

Kaos GL's report 'A Major Siege against LGBTI+ People in 2025: Hostility Turned into State Policy' records six right-to-life violations in 2025, three of them counted as hate-motivated killings, with trans people the most affected. Because the state keeps no official hate-crime statistics, these figures are compiled from media and civil-society reports. The same report documents 89 torture or ill-treatment violations, up from 51 the previous year, mostly linked to peaceful assembly, alongside 336 assembly violations and 313 liberty violations — the liberty figure roughly 2.5 times the prior total, driven mostly by detentions — together with event-specific bans and violent police attacks on peaceful gatherings.

Kaos GL presents this hostility as institutionalised under 'Year of the Family' instructions issued to public institutions, accompanied by hate speech from senior officials, censored broadcasts and cancelled artistic events. The report frames these as national practice rather than provincial choice, and no Ağrı-specific finding appears in it.
tangentialFactors:
The national pattern documented by Kaos GL and Human Rights Watch applies uniformly across Türkiye's provinces, including Ağrı, because the drivers are central government instructions, national legislation and national police practice rather than local policy.

Detention risk is concentrated at public gatherings and street-level identity checks rather than at fixed sites a visitor can avoid by itinerary; the 2025 liberty-violation surge was driven mostly by detentions during assemblies.

The pending status of the 11th Judicial Package does not reliably indicate present safety: reporting from other Turkish cities in 2025 shows police applying the package's prohibitions as though already in force, so a visitor should treat the draft's conduct standards as operationally live.
localsOnly:
Residents of Ağrı live under the same national framework as visitors, but face additional exposure through employment, residence registration and access to public services, none of which the source inventory addresses specifically for the province.

Kaos GL's counts of torture, assembly and liberty violations are compiled from media and civil-society reporting because Türkiye maintains no official hate-crime statistics; local documentation efforts therefore shape what is visible.

The 'Year of the Family' instructions run to public institutions nationwide, which shapes how municipal and provincial offices in Ağrı are directed to treat LGBT matters, though the inventory records no Ağrı-specific implementation.
outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory contains no Ağrı-specific incident, arrest, ordinance or enforcement record; the province-level picture is unresolved and rests entirely on the national framework.

Whether the 11th Judicial Package has been enacted, amended or withdrawn since the 29 October 2025 reporting is unresolved in the sources provided.

The practical effect of the reported Health Ministry restriction on gender-affirming care records in Ağrı facilities is not sourced; no provincial health-directorate reporting for Ağrı appears in the inventory.

Local police practice in Ağrı, including any use of identity checks comparable to those documented in Istanbul, is not sourced and remains unresolved.
